what_its_for: Atropine is used for several different purposes depending on how it is given. It can slow down a very slow heart rate, treat certain types of poisoning (such as from pesticides or nerve agents), reduce saliva and secretions before surgery, treat stomach cramps and spasms, and as eye drops to dilate your pupils for eye exams or to treat certain eye conditions.
how_to_take: Atropine comes in different forms: injections (given by a healthcare provider), eye drops, and tablets. If you are using eye drops, tilt your head back, pull down your lower eyelid to form a small pocket, and place the prescribed number of drops inside. Close your eye gently for 1 to 2 minutes. Press lightly on the inner corner of your eye to stop the medicine from draining away. Do not touch the dropper tip to your eye or any surface. If you are taking tablets, swallow them whole with a full glass of water with or without food. Always follow exactly what your doctor or pharmacist told you.
dosing: Your dose will depend on why you are taking atropine, your age, your weight, and your medical condition. Eye drops are usually 1 drop in the affected eye 1 to 3 times daily as directed. Tablets for stomach issues are usually taken 3 to 4 times a day. Injections are given by a healthcare provider in a hospital or emergency setting. Never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store atropine tablets and eye drops at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep them away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store them in the bathroom. Keep the bottle or container tightly closed when not in use. Keep all forms of atropine out of reach of children and pets. Do not use if the solution looks cloudy or has changed color.
what_to_avoid: Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing any activity that requires clear vision or sharp alertness until you know how atropine affects you, because it can cause blurred vision and dizziness. Avoid getting overheated or doing strenuous exercise in hot weather because atropine reduces your ability to sweat, which can lead to overheating. Avoid alcohol, as it can increase dizziness and drowsiness. Do not wear contact lenses while using atropine eye drops. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you take, especially antihistamines, antidepressants, or bladder medications, as these can increase side effects.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the nearest emergency room if you experience: fast or irregular heartbeat, difficulty urinating or cannot urinate at all, severe constipation, high fever or hot and dry skin (signs of overheating), confusion, hallucinations, severe eye pain or sudden vision changes, rash or signs of an allergic reaction (swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, difficulty breathing). Also call your doctor if your symptoms do not improve or get worse.
when_it_works: How quickly atropine works depends on how it is given. When injected in an emergency, it works within a few minutes to speed up your heart rate. Eye drops usually start dilating your pupils within 30 to 60 minutes, and the effects on your vision may last for several hours to a few days. Tablets for stomach cramps may take 30 to 60 minutes to start working. Your doctor will let you know what to expect based on your specific situation.
special_populations: Older adults: Use with extra caution as atropine can cause increased confusion, memory problems, falls, and difficulty urinating in elderly patients. Children: Dosing must be carefully calculated by a doctor based on the child's weight. Children are more sensitive to the effects of atropine and should be monitored closely. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding before using atropine. It should only be used if clearly needed and under close medical supervision. Patients with glaucoma, enlarged prostate, or certain heart conditions: Tell your doctor about these conditions before starting atropine, as it may not be safe for you.
